meta.titre: Plate Tectonics and Sea Floor Spreading: evidence, plate boundaries and spreading-rate calculations
tags: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

sections.contenu_markdown: Cameroon lies on the African plate. To the west, across the Atlantic Ocean, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is still making new ocean floor, and to the east the continent is slowly splitting along the East African Rift. The same theory explains why earthquakes and volcanoes occur in belts, where fold mountains rise and why the ocean floor is young. Examiners ask you to define sea-floor spreading and plate tectonics, to classify plates and boundaries, to discuss destructive boundaries, and to use evidence and simple data such as the age and distance of ocean-floor rocks.

items: The Earth has a crust, a mantle and a core, and the mantle is hot and moves very slowly.
Basalt is a dark, dense igneous rock; granite is a lighter igneous rock rich in silica.
Earthquakes are caused by sudden movement along faults, and volcanoes erupt where magma reaches the surface.
Speed is distance divided by time.

sections.titre: Plate tectonics: evidence, sea-floor spreading and plate boundaries
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Lithosphere and plates
The **lithosphere** is the crust together with the rigid uppermost mantle, around 100 km thick on average. It is broken into plates that move over the weaker, slowly flowing **asthenosphere**. Oceanic crust is thin (about 7 km), dense and basaltic; continental crust is thicker (about 35 km on average), less dense and granitic in composition. Plates carry the continents and move by a few centimetres a year. Mantle convection, **slab pull** (the weight of the sinking plate, usually regarded as the most important force) and **ridge push** drive the motion.

A plate may be wholly oceanic or may carry a continent. The Nazca and Cocos plates are entirely oceanic, and the Pacific plate is almost entirely oceanic. The African, South American, North American, Eurasian and Antarctic plates all carry continents.

### Evidence for sea-floor spreading
**Sea-floor spreading**: new oceanic lithosphere forms at mid-ocean ridges and moves away on both sides.
- Ocean-floor rocks are youngest at the ridge and become older symmetrically away from it; no ocean floor is older than about 200 million years.
- **Magnetic stripes**: basalt records the Earth's magnetic field as it cools, and as the field reverses from time to time the sea floor shows symmetrical bands of normal and reversed magnetism on either side of the ridge.
- Sediment is thin at the ridge and thickens away from it; heat flow is high at the ridge.
- Evidence for drifting continents: the fit of continental margins, matching rocks and fossils on both sides of the Atlantic, and ancient glacial deposits on continents now far apart.

### Plate boundaries
| Boundary | Movement | Processes and features |
|---|---|---|
| Constructive (divergent) | plates move apart | mantle rock rises and melts as pressure falls; basalt lava; ridge and rift valley; shallow earthquakes |
| Destructive (convergent) | plates move together; denser oceanic lithosphere sinks (subduction) | trench; earthquakes along the Benioff zone down to about 700 km; volcanic arc or island arc; fold mountains |
| Conservative (transform) | plates slide past each other | shallow earthquakes only; no volcanoes; crust neither made nor destroyed |

At a destructive boundary, water released from the sinking slab lowers the melting point of the mantle above it, and the magma that forms rises to give explosive andesitic volcanoes. When two continents collide, neither sinks easily because continental crust is buoyant, so the crust thickens and fold mountains and thrust faults develop.

variantes.nom: Define sea-floor spreading and plate tectonics
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks what is meant by these concepts.
variantes.contenu_markdown: **Sea-floor spreading** is the process by which new oceanic lithosphere forms at mid-ocean ridges, as magma rises and solidifies, and moves away from the ridge on both sides. **Plate tectonics** is the theory that the lithosphere is divided into rigid plates that move relative to one another, and that most earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain building happen at plate margins. Add one example or piece of evidence to each definition.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to discuss the processes and features of plate convergence.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Organise by type: ocean-continent (trench, volcanic arc on the continent, fold mountains, such as the Andes), ocean-ocean (trench and island arc) and continent-continent (collision, thickened crust, fold mountains such as the Himalayas). In each case give the process first (subduction, melting, compression), then the feature it produces (earthquakes, volcanoes, mountains).

variantes.quand_utiliser: When distance and age of ocean-floor rock are given.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Rate $=$ distance $\div$ age. Convert with $1\ \mathrm{km\,Ma^{-1}} = 1\ \mathrm{mm\,yr^{-1}}$. The distance from the ridge axis to one side gives the half rate; the two plates separate at twice that value (the full rate). Assume a constant rate unless the question says otherwise.

sections.enonce_markdown: A survey across a mid-ocean ridge finds magnetic stripes that are symmetrical about the ridge axis. Basalt of age $10.0$ million years lies $250\ \mathrm{km}$ east of the axis, and a matching stripe lies at the same distance west of it. (a) Calculate the half spreading rate and the full spreading rate in $\mathrm{cm\,yr^{-1}}$. (b) Predict the age of basalt $700\ \mathrm{km}$ from the axis. (c) Calculate how long an ocean basin $4000\ \mathrm{km}$ wide would take to open at this rate. (d) Explain how the magnetic stripes support sea-floor spreading.

etapes.justification: Speed is distance divided by time, and the basalt 250 km from the axis formed at the axis 10.0 million years ago.
The two plates move away from the ridge in opposite directions, so they separate at twice the half rate.
At a constant half rate, age equals distance from the axis divided by the half rate.

etapes.action: Calculate the opening time of the basin.
etapes.justification: The full width opens at the full rate.

etapes.action: Explain the evidence of the magnetic stripes.
etapes.justification: Basalt that cools at the ridge records the direction of the Earth's magnetic field, and the field reverses from time to time.
etapes.resultat_markdown: New basalt forms in the centre and splits to both sides, so symmetrical stripes of normal and reversed magnetism and symmetrical ages show that the floor grew outwards from the ridge.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The half rate is $2.5\ \mathrm{cm\,yr^{-1}}$ and the full rate $5.0\ \mathrm{cm\,yr^{-1}}$; basalt at $700\ \mathrm{km}$ should be about $28\ \mathrm{Ma}$ old; the basin would open in about $80\ \mathrm{Ma}$; and the symmetrical stripes and ages show that new ocean floor is made at the ridge and moves away.

items.erreur_markdown: "Continents plough through the solid ocean floor."
items.pourquoi_faux: Continents do not move through the ocean floor; they are embedded in plates and are carried along with them.
items.correction_markdown: Say that plates carry the continents and that new oceanic lithosphere forms at the ridge.

items.erreur_markdown: "A plate is the same thing as the crust."
items.pourquoi_faux: A plate is lithosphere, which is the crust together with the rigid uppermost mantle.
items.correction_markdown: Define plates as pieces of lithosphere moving over the asthenosphere.

items.erreur_markdown: "The oldest oceanic crust is found at the mid-ocean ridge."
items.pourquoi_faux: The ridge is where new crust is made, so the rocks there are the youngest and the age increases away from the ridge.
items.correction_markdown: State that ocean-floor age increases symmetrically on both sides of the ridge.

items.erreur_markdown: "Continental crust is subducted at every convergent boundary."
items.pourquoi_faux: Continental crust is less dense and buoyant, so it resists subduction. Where two continents meet, the crust thickens and mountains rise.
items.correction_markdown: Subduction involves oceanic lithosphere; continental collision gives fold mountains and thrusting.

items.erreur_markdown: "The Earth is getting bigger because new crust forms at ridges."
items.pourquoi_faux: New crust at ridges is balanced by lithosphere destroyed at subduction zones, so the total surface area does not increase.
items.correction_markdown: Say that creation of lithosphere at constructive boundaries is balanced by destruction at destructive boundaries.

items.enonce_markdown: Boundary X shows basalt lava, a rift valley and shallow earthquakes. Boundary Y shows an ocean trench, andesitic volcanoes and earthquakes as deep as $600\ \mathrm{km}$. Boundary Z shows only shallow earthquakes, no volcanoes and a ridge offset sideways. (a) Name the type of each boundary. (b) State whether each of the Nazca, African and Eurasian plates is entirely oceanic or carries a continent.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **X: constructive (divergent)**, where plates move apart and new crust forms. **Y: destructive (convergent)**, with subduction along a Benioff zone. **Z: conservative (transform)**, where plates slide past one another.

(b) **Nazca: entirely oceanic.** **African and Eurasian: each carries a continent.**

items.enonce_markdown: Basalt $8.0$ million years old lies $160\ \mathrm{km}$ from the ridge axis on both sides of a mid-ocean ridge. (a) Calculate the half rate and the full rate in $\mathrm{cm\,yr^{-1}}$. (b) Calculate the age of basalt $550\ \mathrm{km}$ from the axis. (c) How far from the axis would basalt $35$ million years old be found?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Half rate $= \dfrac{160}{8.0} = 20\ \mathrm{km\,Ma^{-1}} = $ **$2.0\ \mathrm{cm\,yr^{-1}}$**, so the full rate is **$4.0\ \mathrm{cm\,yr^{-1}}$**.

(b) Age $= \dfrac{550}{20} = $ **27.5 Ma**.

(c) Distance $= 20\times35 = $ **$700\ \mathrm{km}$**.

items.enonce_markdown: An oceanic plate descends beneath a continent along a slab that dips at a constant $45^\circ$. (a) An earthquake focus lies in the slab at a depth of $400\ \mathrm{km}$. Calculate its distance along the slab from the surface. (b) Assume that the slab moves along its length at the convergence rate of $6.0\ \mathrm{cm\,yr^{-1}}$. Calculate how long the plate takes to sink to this depth. (c) Explain why andesitic volcanoes form on the continent above the slab.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Distance along the slab $= \dfrac{400}{\sin 45^\circ} = $ **$566\ \mathrm{km}$** (565.7 km).

(b) $6.0\ \mathrm{cm\,yr^{-1}} = 60\ \mathrm{km\,Ma^{-1}}$, so the time is $\dfrac{565.7}{60} = $ **9.4 Ma**.

(c) The descending slab carries water in wet sediment and altered basalt. At depth the water is released into the mantle above, lowering its melting point so that it partly melts. The magma rises, and as it crosses the continental crust it evolves to a silica-rich andesitic composition, which is viscous and gas-rich and erupts explosively.

items_markdown: The lithosphere (crust plus rigid upper mantle) is divided into plates that move over the asthenosphere, driven by mantle convection, slab pull and ridge push.
Sea-floor spreading makes new oceanic lithosphere at ridges; evidence is the symmetrical age pattern, symmetrical magnetic stripes, thin sediment at the ridge and high heat flow.
Plates may be wholly oceanic (Nazca, Cocos) or carry a continent (African, South American, Eurasian and others).

Constructive boundaries make crust (basalt, ridge, rift valley); destructive boundaries destroy it (trench, Benioff zone, volcanic arc, fold mountains); conservative boundaries only shear (shallow earthquakes).
Subduction melting starts when water from the slab lowers the melting point of the mantle wedge; continental collision does not subduct because continental crust is buoyant.
Spreading rate $=$ distance $\div$ age; $1\ \mathrm{km\,Ma^{-1}} = 1\ \mathrm{mm\,yr^{-1}}$, and the full rate is twice the half rate.
